Migration 0008 — the reaction event table and its per-person fold
I hit the tool-use limit mid-slice, so I don't have a deliverable archive for you yet. Here's where things stand.

What I verified
Tree reconstruction from dump.txt: 370 files, SHA-256 checked one by one. 369 verified clean. The two differences are both by design — export.sh embeds its own file marker (so my parser can't reproduce it), and LICENSE is elided to metadata and hash. The final file in the dump needed the trailer stripped before it hashed correctly; it does. No session drift in the tree itself.

My session memory was stale by two slices, and the tree corrected it. I came in believing Slice 54 (picture history) was the most recent with ~1250 predicted against an unverified 1242 baseline. The tree is at Slice 56, and claude-terminal.txt shows the run: total: 1260, failed: 0, plus 20 E2E green, ci_local.sh --with-all --with-e2e clear. Slice 56 predicted 1260 and got 1260.

I rebuilt the test-count arithmetic model and it is exact. Counting [Fact] methods, [InlineData] rows, and the two [MemberData] sources in SchemaMigrationRunnerTests gives 910 + 329 + 21 = 1260, matching your terminal to the unit. That gives a reliable prediction instrument for §18.

Where the plan actually is
Stage 4 closed completely in Slice 56 — F-108 (the stackalloc CA2014 build break), F-109 (bytes decide the media type), F-110 (the format census derived rather than spelled). The plan's own words: "Stage 4's open list is empty for the first time since 4a." Next is Stage 5 — likes, which the plan says needs two rulings before it ships.

The rulings I settled, and why
Who sees the count → staff. The plan's own instinct was right: a count of 3 on a menu of sixty items makes a restaurant look empty. So the write is a guest action and the read is an administration read — which is exactly order_visibility_event's split (a guest hides, an administrator sees the hidden-records page). The guest still needs their own heart state back, so that's a per-person boolean and the staff count is an aggregate; two reads over one fold.

Does a like require having ordered the item → no, and the reason is that the check cannot be made true. order_current_line records what a person ordered, not what they ate, and a table shares — so the requirement would refuse the case it most wants (I ate my partner's dessert) while admitting the one it wants to refuse. It would also make a menu write read order history, inverting §6.5.4's direction. The mechanism if it's ever wanted is named rather than hand-waved: it belongs in a second count on the read side, not in the write.

A reaction publishes nothing. §9's MenuChanged means re-read the menu, and the menu has not changed. This is the one write in the application that can fire many times a minute at one table; broadcasting would make a heart-tap re-read the whole menu on every phone in the building. Which means it is also the first menu write not behind IMenuWorkflow — stated as an exception with its reason, and MenuWiringTests' "covers every write service" sentence narrows to "every write service that changes the menu."

What I'd written before the limit
Only 0008_menu_item_reactions.sql: the event table (two types, no payload columns, so no paired biconditional), a named vocabulary constraint on 0006's rule, one index whose column order is the fold's prefix, and menu_item_reaction_current as a DISTINCT ON (menu_item_identifier, person_identifier) fold. Both foreign keys are real — unlike menu_item_image_event's bare uuid — which is what makes TRUNCATE … CASCADE reach this table and OrderTestWorld need no edit.

The one thing in it worth flagging now: the identifier tie-break in that view is load-bearing here in a way it is not on order_visibility_current. Hiding an order twice in a millisecond is a thing nobody does. Double-tapping a heart is a thing everybody does, and one transaction stamps its rows with one IClock.UtcNow — so without the tie-break, DISTINCT ON returns the oldest row and a double-tap reads back as the state before it. That only works because F-95 made IIdentifierFactory ascend within a millisecond. It's the fact this slice contributes that nothing else in the tree has, and it gets an integration assertion.

Say "go" and I'll deliver
Next response, the full archive: the migration above, MenuItemReactions.cs (read + write, FOR UPDATE on menu_item before the comparison per standing convention), the DI registration, nine integration facts in MenuItemReactionTests.cs, the wiring fact, two KeyRelations rows, and every document — spec to v1.42 with §7/§8.2/§8.3/§16.4/Appendix A/changelog, plus DOCUMENTATION_REVIEW.md, MENU_AND_HANDHELD_PLAN.md, BUILD_PROGRESS.md whole, and _CHANGES.md. Predicted count 1272 (nine new facts + one wiring fact + two theory rows), stated properly with the arithmetic table before delivery. No deletes expected; the new files needing git add will be listed explicitly.

Nothing to delete. Those three are the only new files.

Predicted test count: 1273, recomputed from the edited tree rather than carried — 921 facts + 329 inline rows + 23 member-data rows. I told you 1272 last message; that estimate dropped an increment and _CHANGES.md says so plainly rather than fixing it quietly. §16.3 stays at twenty, since 5a builds no surface.

Both of Stage 5's rulings are made. The count is staff-facing — 3 on a menu of sixty makes a restaurant look empty, so which of these is popular is §11.4's question and which of these do I like is §11.1's, two reads over one fold. And a like requires only a person: order_current_line records what somebody ordered, not what they ate, and a table shares, so the restriction would refuse the case it most wants (I ate my partner's dessert) while inverting §6.5.4's direction. It stays reversible additively — if it's ever wanted it belongs on the read as a narrower count.

One fact carries this slice. TwoPressesAtOneInstantFoldToTheLater. Nobody hides an order twice in a millisecond, so order_visibility_current's tie-break has never had to work. Everybody taps a heart twice, and one transaction stamps one IClock.UtcNow — so without the tie-break DISTINCT ON returns the oldest row and a double-tap reads back as the state before it. It's only an answer because F-95 made the identifier factory ascend inside a millisecond.

F-111, found opening §8.2 to add a table to it. The note under menu_item_event's DDL described five event types and two payload columns, twelve lines below a block correctly showing eight and five — and required "integration tests must assert all ten combinations", an obligation whose arithmetic was wrong even for the schema it was written against, and which §16.4 separately rules against writing (F-47). One section required tests another forbade; the tree obeyed the second. Counts deleted, obligation reversed, and the quotation made executable: a fourth fact holding every named event_type vocabulary the spec quotes against the migrations, both directions, subject computed on each side. Proven sensitive three ways.

Three veto points, each reversible alone: the FOR UPDATE on menu_item is wider than the conflict it guards; IMenuItemReactions sits outside IMenuWorkflow (the first menu write that does); and the new gate reads a 609 KiB document on every unit run. Reversion instructions are in _CHANGES.md.

Two notes on what I couldn't check. Nothing was compiled — no SDK here — and the one call shape with no exact precedent is ExecuteScalarAsync<Guid?> against a SELECT … FOR UPDATE; if it misbehaves it does so as a null where an identifier belongs, which one of the nine facts reaches from the wrong side. Also worth knowing: my session memory opened two slices stale, believing the tree was at Slice 54 against an unverified 1242. The SHA-256 reconstruction caught it before anything was authored — fourth drift event this log records.

Stage 5b is two surfaces with no decisions left in them: §11.4's count on the menu index, §11.1's control in the detail panel (the panel, not the card — the card is already a button).
